claim: Every global minimum-q square-only selection is unicyclic in each component.
review: If any global minimum-q selection contains two square blocks in one component, minimise their distance over the entire finite family of offending minimum-q selections. The three previously accepted moves either reduce q or reduce this distance, including incident distance zero. This rules out all offending selections, not just one selected normal form. The exact defect q=c then excludes tree components.

claim: All eligible edges of a cycle colour stay in its square component.
review: Both selected occurrences of that colour belong to its square. A path in another component avoids that colour, ruling out an eligible edge internal to that component. A cross-component edge replaces one square edge, breaks precisely that cycle and joins two components without a new cycle. This contradicts global minimality of q.

claim: All full-graph neighbours of square vertices stay in its component.
review: A commuting generator outside the square colours lies in the omitted-generator subgroup, preserving each orbit, and transports the relevant eligible edge. The only noncommuting-by-index possibility is the middle colour between square colours i-1,i+1. Removing the transported square leaves four trees in the transported component. An inserted original square vertex in another component would connect the new square to the unchanged old square of that component, contradicting Lemma1.

claim: An ordinary slide preserves all component vertex sets.
review: Localisation puts both added edges in the old component. An outside removed edge would be a bridge because its other selected colour occurrence already lies in the first component. Deleting it leaves a tree untouched by insertion, forbidden by Lemma1. All edits are therefore internal; the sole new square cannot populate two components, so no disconnection is possible.

claim: The global middle move transports the partition.
review: The four inserted square vertices lie in the transported original component, by Lemma3. Every tree left on deleting its square must be rejoined; otherwise a tree component remains. Other components are untouched transported components. This establishes the image partition, not invariance under the generator.

claim: Every minimum-q equality selection is connected, hence has one square.
review: If one is connected then q=1 and Lemma1 settles every other one. Otherwise choose globally shortest connector with one unselected cross-edge. Lemma3 makes both selected tails nonempty. For an ordinary first colour ell, if its other selected occurrence lies later on either tail, the two sides of the first bridge exclude w-prime: the forward side has no a-edges; the backward side has no ell-edges. This works with the second ell-edge in the other component as well. Localisation contradicts w-prime outside the component. The slide thus preserves the rest of the connector and shortens it. Both endpoints must instead be middle colours. The two square-colour sets are disjoint, so choose an endpoint whose square colours omit the cross-edge colour x. Its middle generator commutes with x, including equality. Global transport preserves an actual cross-edge between the two transported components, all remaining selected edges, and the other square. Removing the first edge shortens the connector; any new incidental square contact only shortens further.
